what_its_for: Danazol is used to treat endometriosis (a condition where tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus), fibrocystic breast disease (non-cancerous lumps in the breasts), and to prevent attacks of hereditary angioedema (a condition that causes sudden swelling in parts of the body). It works by reducing the amount of certain hormones made by your body.
how_to_take: Take danazol by mouth with a full glass of water. You can take it with or without food, but taking it with food may help reduce stomach upset. Try to take it at the same times each day to keep a steady amount of the medicine in your body. Swallow the capsules whole — do not crush or chew them. Keep taking danazol even if you feel well, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your condition. Typical doses range from 50 mg to 800 mg per day, usually divided into 2 doses taken morning and evening. For endometriosis, treatment usually lasts 3 to 6 months, and sometimes up to 9 months. For fibrocystic breast disease, treatment is usually 3 to 6 months. For hereditary angioedema, your doctor may start with a higher dose and then lower it once your condition is controlled. Always follow your doctor's specific dosing instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not double up or take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store danazol capsules at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C and 30°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to safely dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Do not take danazol if you are pregnant or trying to become pregnant, as it can cause serious harm to a developing baby. Use a non-hormonal form of birth control (such as condoms or a diaphragm) during treatment — do not rely on birth control pills, as danazol may make them less effective. Avoid drinking alcohol, as it may worsen side effects. Avoid activities that require alertness if you feel dizzy or drowsy. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you take, especially blood thinners like warfarin, diabetes medicines, or cholesterol-lowering drugs, as danazol can interact with many medications.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or seek emergency medical help if you experience: signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, severe stomach pain, or unusual tiredness; signs of blood clots such as chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, leg swelling or pain; signs of a stroke such as sudden severe headache, vision changes, weakness on one side of the body, or difficulty speaking; unusual weight gain or swelling; voice changes or hoarseness (especially in women); increased hair growth, acne, or enlarged clitoris; depression, mood changes, or unusual thoughts; irregular or stopped menstrual periods that do not return after finishing treatment; or any allergic reaction such as rash, itching, or swelling of the face or throat.
when_it_works: You may not notice improvement right away. For endometriosis and fibrocystic breast disease, it may take several weeks to a few months before you feel significant relief from pain or other symptoms. Your menstrual period may stop during treatment, which is expected and part of how the medicine works. For hereditary angioedema, it may take a few days to a couple of weeks to notice fewer attacks. Do not stop taking danazol without talking to your doctor, even if you do not notice improvement right away.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Danazol must NOT be used during pregnancy. It can cause serious birth defects, especially in female babies (such as abnormal development of genitals). A pregnancy test should be done before starting treatment, and reliable non-hormonal birth control must be used throughout therapy. Breastfeeding: Do not use danazol while breastfeeding, as it may pass into breast milk and harm the baby. Children: Safety and effectiveness in children have not been fully established. Use with caution as it may affect growth and development. Older adults: Use with caution in older patients, who may be more sensitive to side effects. Liver, kidney, or heart disease: Danazol should generally not be used in people with severe liver, kidney, or heart problems. Tell your doctor about all your medical conditions before starting this medicine.
